We ate takoyaki and shaved ice.

The goldfish seemed to be watching the fireworks too.

I work from ten at night until six in the morning.
At twelve midnight, an old man comes.
He always buys milk and one meat bun.
But today he bought two meat buns.
I said, "Two today, huh."

"Thanks as always. Good luck with your night work."

It was a cold night outside, but my heart became warm too.

sents.en: In autumn, I went on a trip to Kyoto by myself.
I was planning to go see a famous temple listed in my guidebook.
But while walking along narrow streets, I ended up getting lost.

tok.s: まよってしまいました

sents.en: Even looking at the map, I couldn't tell where I was.
Just then, an old woman from a small sweet shop called out to me.
"Where do you want to go?"
When I said the temple's name, she laughed and said, "There are a lot of people there today."
And then she told me about a small temple behind her shop.
There was no one there.
The maple leaves in the garden were bright red, and it was very quiet.
I sat there for a long time.
On the way back, I bought sweets at the old woman's shop.
I couldn't go to the famous temple, but that became my best memory.

Fuji at dawn, a father and his teenage child in hiking jackets and headlamps standing on dark volcanic rock above an endless sea of clouds glowing pink, orange and gold, the brilliant sun just breaking through a gap in the clouds, the father holding out a faded old photograph toward the child, other climbers silhouetted in the distance raising their arms, crisp cold air and a sense of awe and quiet emotion. sents.en: During summer vacation, I climbed Mt. Fuji with my father.
We left the mountain hut at two in the middle of the night and walked slowly along the dark path.
The air was thin, and I got very tired.
"Almost there," my father said again and again.
Around four-thirty in the morning, we finally reached the summit.
But the eastern sky was covered with thick clouds.
I was disappointed and looked down.
Just then, the people around us cried out, "Ah!"
A golden sun had come out from a gap in the clouds.
The sea of clouds was shining pink and orange.
My father took an old photo out of his pocket.
It was a photo of my father and mother, taken here thirty years ago.
"I proposed to your mom right here," my father said with a laugh.
This time, I was the one who took a photo of my father.

title: 二十歳の わたしへ
img: A small desk by a window at night in a cozy Japanese apartment, a young woman of twenty sitting under a warm desk lamp drawing a cute cat in a new sketchbook with a pencil, beside her an old rust-spotted tin time-capsule box and an unfolded childhood letter covered in large clumsy handwriting shapes and a crayon cat doodle, a mug of tea steaming, city lights and a crescent moon outside, quiet, hopeful, nostalgic mood. sents.en: When I was ten, I wrote "A Letter to Myself Ten Years From Now" at school.
We put the letters in a time capsule and buried it in the schoolyard.
And this year, now twenty, we gathered at the school.
The box that came out of the ground was a little rusty.
The handwriting in my letter was big and clumsy.
"Dear me at twenty. Are you still drawing pictures?"
I couldn't answer.

tok.s: 答えられませんでした
tok.r: こたえられませんでした

sents.en: That's because after starting university, I got busy and quit drawing.
At the end of the letter, there was a clumsy drawing of a cat.
Under it was written, "Someday I want to make a cat book!"
On the way home, I bought a small notebook and a pencil at a shop in the station.
That night, I drew a cat for the first time in ten years.
And then I began writing a new letter to myself at thirty.
"Dear me at thirty. Is the cat book finished?"

sents.en: During spring break, I rode the shinkansen by myself for the first time.

sents.en: On Friday afternoon, I lost my wallet.

I wrote a thank-you card to the boy and left it at the police box.

title: おじいちゃんの 古い カメラ
img: A traditional Japanese countryside house on a bright summer day, an elderly couple sitting side by side on the wooden engawa veranda smiling shyly at the camera, their teenage grandchild crouching in the garden aiming a vintage black film camera at them, lush green trees, a glass wind chime and a bamboo blind hanging from the eaves, morning glories climbing a trellis, a few faded sepia photographs of a laughing young woman at the seaside laid out on the veranda boards beside an old camera case, warm dappled sunlight, nostalgic and tender mood. Painted in a consistent warm, hand-painted Studio-Ghibli-inspired watercolor style: soft edges, gentle textured paper, rich but soft colors, cozy nostalgic atmosphere. No text, letters, signs with writing, or captions anywhere in the image.

sents.en: During summer vacation, I went to visit Grandpa's house in the countryside.
While I was looking through the closet, an old black camera turned up.
"How nostalgic! That's the camera I always carried around when I was young," Grandpa said.
It's an old-fashioned camera that you load with film to take pictures.
When I looked closely, there was still film inside, and it seemed there was just one shot left.
"I don't remember at all what I took," Grandpa laughed.
So I used the last shot to take a picture of Grandpa and Grandma.
The two of them sat side by side on the veranda and smiled a little shyly.
The next day, I took the film to the photo shop in town.
A week later, we looked at the finished photos and were amazed.
They were full of Grandma at twenty, laughing by the sea and in the mountains.
"These are from the year I first went on a date with Grandma," Grandpa said, his face turning red.
And the very last photo was the one of the two of them taken on the veranda.
On the same roll of film were the two of them fifty years ago and the two of them now.
Grandma laughed, "This film took fifty years to finish, didn't it."

title: ラーメン屋の アルバイト
img: A small cozy ramen shop late at night after closing time, warm lamplight glowing over a worn wooden counter, a stern older ramen chef in a white towel headband and apron sitting at the counter tipping up a big bowl to drink the last of the soup, a nervous young university student in an apron standing behind the counter watching his face anxiously, steaming stockpots and neatly stacked bowls, a plain indigo noren curtain with no writing hanging in the doorway, a bicycle parked outside under a streetlamp, quiet, tense-but-warm mood. Painted in a consistent warm, hand-painted Studio-Ghibli-inspired watercolor style: soft edges, gentle textured paper, rich but soft colors, cozy nostalgic atmosphere. No text, letters, signs with writing, or captions anywhere in the image.

sents.en: After I started university, I began a part-time job at a small ramen shop near the station.
The owner is a man of about sixty who doesn't talk much.
My job was washing bowls and carrying ramen to the customers.
The owner comes to the shop at five every morning and makes the soup.
I hear it takes ten whole hours to make the soup.
After the shop closed, the owner always made ramen for me.
It's called "makanai," a meal for the people who work at the shop.
One night, after three months had passed, the owner said, "Today, you try making it."
Just as I had always watched him do, I carefully boiled the noodles and poured in the soup.
Without saying a word, the owner began to eat the ramen.
With my heart pounding, I watched his face.
After drinking all of the soup, the owner said, "Still a long way to go."

tok.g: still a long way to go

sents.en: As I was feeling disappointed, the owner smiled a little and said:
"But your noodle boiling passes. From tomorrow, I'm leaving the noodles to you."
That night, I smiled the whole way home on my bicycle.

sents.en: Dad, Mom, Grandma, how are you?
It's already been a month since I came to Japan.
My host family, the Yamadas, live in a small town near the sea.
Every morning, Mrs. Yamada makes me a delicious breakfast.
At first I couldn't eat natto, but now I love it.

sents.en: My friends at school all talk fast, and at first I couldn't understand anything.
But one day, a girl in my class said to me, "Let's eat lunch together."
Since then, we've been walking home together every day.
Last week, at the town's summer festival, I wore a yukata for the first time.
By the way, do you know why I wrote this letter in Japanese?
It's because I wanted you, Grandma, to read my Japanese.
Grandma, you went from Japan to Brazil when you were a child, didn't you?
I still remember the Japanese song you taught me when I was little.
Actually, I found out that the village where you were born is just an hour from this town by train!
Next month, I'll go to that village with the Yamadas and send you lots of photos.
From Maria
